title: Three machines in bypass
note: Fictional unit. The machine’s service manual, your unit’s procedure, and the formal release process come first.
intro: You are the biomedical technician. At 06:25 on Tuesday, the charge nurse calls you: three machines in different rows, HD-02, HD-07, and HD-13, are alarming for conductivity and going in and out of bypass. No patient is connected yet; the first shift starts at 06:45. The central acid concentrate tank was refilled from a new delivery at 05:50.

choices.text: The shared supply: check the central tank, the new batch and its label, and hold connections on machines fed by it.
choices.feedback: Read the pattern before you touch a machine. One machine with a problem points to that machine; several machines at once point to something they share.
choices.then: The new drums are labeled for a different proportioning system from the one your machines are configured for. The tank was filled with the wrong product.

choices.text: Start with HD-02 and work through each machine’s conductivity calibration, since all three are the same model and may share a fault.
choices.feedback: Three machines failing together are very unlikely to have three separate sensor faults. Recalibrating them to the wrong fluid would teach them to accept it.
choices.then: You check the central tank instead. The new drums are labeled for a different proportioning system. The tank was filled with the wrong product.

choices.text: Override the bypass on the three machines so the shift can start on time.
choices.feedback: Bypass is the safe state: the machine is saying it does not trust the fluid. Overriding it sends fluid of unknown composition to the patient’s dialyzer.
choices.then: The charge nurse refuses. You check the central tank: the new drums are labeled for a different proportioning system.

choices.text: Hold the central supply and the batch with its lot numbers, report it, and refill with the verified product by procedure.
choices.feedback: The batch and labels are evidence, and no machine runs on that supply until it is corrected. The charge nurse decides what happens to the shift; your job is to make the fluid right and say when it is.
choices.then: The tank is drained, rinsed, and refilled with the correct product by procedure. By 07:30, HD-02, HD-07, and HD-13 stabilize and pass their checks.

choices.text: Top up the tank with the correct product; it will dilute the wrong one.
choices.feedback: A mixture of two products is a third, unknown fluid. The tank is emptied and refilled with the right product by procedure.
choices.then: The chief technician has the tank drained, rinsed, and refilled. By 07:30 the three machines stabilize and pass their checks.

choices.text: Switch the three machines to individual jugs of the correct concentrate so the shift can start, and deal with the central tank after the shift.
choices.feedback: That can keep treatments going if your procedure allows it, but every machine on the central supply is still exposed. Hold the supply and report it first.
choices.then: The tank is held, drained, and refilled. By 07:30 the three machines stabilize and pass their checks.

n3.scene: Mid-morning, the nurse reports that HD-11, on its own jugs, has read steadily about 3% higher than the machines beside it all week, and alarmed once today. It is taken off the floor for you.
n3.prompt: How do you start the verification?

choices.text: Check the meter against standard today, match reference temperature, let HD-11 stabilize, and sample by the manual.
choices.feedback: A verification is only as good as its reference. An unchecked meter or a temperature mismatch can create a false disagreement of several percent, and you may adjust a correct machine to match a wrong meter.
choices.then: Your meter reads the standard correctly. HD-11’s display reads 2.8% above the reference, outside the manual’s tolerance.

choices.text: Adjust HD-11 to match the reading on the machine next to it.
choices.feedback: Another machine’s display is not a reference. Use a calibrated meter checked against standard solution.
choices.then: You get the reference meter and check it against standard first. HD-11 reads 2.8% above the reference, outside tolerance.

choices.text: Measure with your meter straight away; it was calibrated by the supplier last month and the certificate is still valid.
choices.feedback: Last month’s calibration is not today’s check. Prove the meter against standard solution the same day before you trust it to judge the machine.
choices.then: You check the meter against standard: it reads correctly. HD-11 reads 2.8% above the reference, outside tolerance.

n4.scene: The log shows HD-11’s descaling is overdue, and its readings have drifted up over several weeks.

choices.text: Descale and clean the cells, then verify again; calibrate only if it is still out of tolerance.
choices.feedback: A drift over weeks points to scale on the cells and in the pumps. Clean first; calibration is changed only when a verified reference shows the sensor itself is wrong.
choices.then: After descaling, HD-11 reads within 0.5% of the reference. No calibration change is needed.

choices.text: Widen HD-11’s conductivity alarm limits so it stops alarming.
choices.feedback: Wider limits let fluid of the wrong composition reach the patient, which is exactly what the alarm is for. Never adjust a machine to silence an alarm.
choices.then: You restore the limits and descale the cells by the manual. HD-11 then reads within 0.5% of the reference.

choices.text: Recalibrate the sensor to the reference now, which brings it into tolerance at once, and schedule the descaling for next month.
choices.feedback: Calibrating over scale hides the cause, and the reading drifts again as the scale changes. Clean first, then verify again.
choices.then: You descale first. HD-11 then reads within 0.5% of the reference without a calibration change.

n5.prompt: What remains before HD-11 goes back to the floor?

choices.text: Prove the alarm and bypass by the manual, disinfect, record as-found and as-left, and release formally.
choices.feedback: A correct reading is half the job. The other half is proving that an out-of-range reading really does switch the bypass valve. The record lets the next person see what changed.

choices.text: The reading is correct now, so tell the nurse it is ready.
choices.feedback: A machine is released only after its protective function is proven and recorded, through the formal process.

choices.text: Record the as-left value with the meter’s identity and release it to the nurse, since the reading is now within tolerance.
choices.feedback: Recording matters, but the as-found value, the meter identity, the bypass test, and disinfection are part of the record too.

end.title: End of the day
end.text: The concentrate supplier is notified about the wrong delivery, and the held drums are returned with their lot numbers. The unit adds a label check against the machine configuration before any central tank refill. HD-11’s descaling interval is put back on schedule.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Read the pattern first. Several machines at once: shared concentrate or water.
  • Bypass is the safe state. Never override it to start a shift.
  • A verification is only as good as its reference. Check the meter against standard the same day; match the reference temperature.
  • Clean before you calibrate, and never adjust to silence an alarm.
  • Prove bypass, record as-found and as-left, then release formally.

See Bypass, Verifying conductivity and Troubleshooting.
